units.title: Chapter 1 · Introductory Lesson 1 (Day 1): Greetings and Tagalog sounds

lessons.title: 1. C1 L1 · Greetings, titles and saying who you are
lessons.subtitle: Magandang umaga · po and ho · Ako si · Taga- · Kumusta ka? · naman, rin, din

explanations.title: Four greetings for the time of day
explanations.body: English has three greetings for the time of day; Tagalog has four. The book gives the hours: midnight to 11:59 a.m. is magandang umaga; noon to 12:59 p.m. is magandang tanghali; 1:00 to 5:59 p.m. is magandang hapon; 6:00 to 11:59 p.m. is magandang gabi. Mind the stress: hápon (afternoon) is not Hapón (Japanese). In the video, po is introduced as the formal, polite element.

explanations.title: Titles, po and ho
explanations.body:
Titles: Ginoo (Mr., G.), Binibini (Miss or Ms., Bb.) and Ginang (Mrs., Gng.). Add the linker -ng to Ginoo and Binibini only when they are linked to a name (Ginoong Cruz, Binibing Reyes); the ng in Ginang is not a linker but part of the word. The book spells the titles with abbreviations; the spoken lines here write them out. Filipinos often use the English words as well.

Po and ho show respect for elders, persons of higher rank or authority and new acquaintances. Ho is slightly less formal than po, used with people you are comfortable with; in informal settings they are interchangeable.

explanations.title: Also: naman, rin and din
explanations.body: Naman is an enclitic with many uses; here it means “also/too” in a reply to a greeting. Rin and din both mean “also”: use rin when the word before it ends with a vowel (Magandang tanghali rin) and din when it ends with a consonant (Magandang hapon din). The book says naman will be explained in later units.

examples.translation: Remy: Good morning, sir, Mr. Cruz.
Ginoong Cruz: Good morning to you too, Remy.
Binibining Legazpi: Good noon to you too, Nicko.

explanations.title: Saying who you are and where you are from
explanations.body: Ako si + name means “I am + name”. There is no verb “to be”: the marker si goes in front of a person’s name. To say where you are from, use Taga + place (short answer: “From + place”) or Taga + place + ako (long answer: “I am from + place”). Po or ho goes after the first word or at the end when you speak to a superior.

explanations.title: Practice dialogs
explanations.body: The book’s models for pair work (Activities 4 and 5). Names and places are as in the book; “G. Cruz”, “Gng. Yu” and “Bb. Tilde” are written out in full.

lessons.title: 2. C1 L1 · The alphabet and the Tagalog vowels
lessons.subtitle: Abakada · five vowels · diphthongs · borrowed letters · glottal stops · vowel sequences

explanations.title: The alphabet
explanations.body:
The Tagalog alphabet (traditionally the Abakada) has 28 letters: the 26 English letters plus Ñ (en-yeh) and NG (en-gee). C, F, J, Ñ, Q, V, X and Z are mostly used for names of people and places and for words not native to the language. Tagalog has 16 consonant sounds (counting the glottal stop, shown as a stress mark), 5 vowel sounds and 5 diphthongs. There are no silent letters, and diacritical marks are not used in ordinary writing and printing.

A Aa, B Bb, C Cc, D Dd, E Ee, F Ff, G Gg, H Hh, I Ii, J Jj, K Kk, L Ll, M Mm, N Nn, Ñ ñ, NG ng, O Oo, P Pp, Q Qq, R Rr, S Ss, T Tt, U Uu, V Vv, W Ww, X Xx, Y Yy, Z Zz.

explanations.title: The five vowels
explanations.body: A is as in alms, palm, far; E as in end, pet, set; I as in nip, cliff, hit; O as in obey, order, boy; U as in food, mood, wood.

explanations.title: Diphthongs
explanations.body: The five diphthongs are written iw, uy, oy, ay and aw (plus ey in a few borrowed words).

explanations.title: Letters borrowed from English and Spanish
explanations.body: These letters are used in their original form and pronounced like their English or Spanish counterparts, or they are adapted by changing the spelling: C is K (Castro, Cruz); CH is TS (litson, litsugas, tsinelas); J is J (Joseph, jeep) or H (José, Juan, Jolo); LL is LY (calle, Castillo); Ñ is NY (España, Muñoz, Los Baños); Q(u) is K (Quiapo, Quezon); X is S (Xenia, xylophone) or KS (Ajax, taxi); Z is S (Zamora, Zenaida, Zamboanga).

explanations.title: Glottal stops and vowel sequences
explanations.body:
The acute glottal stop (maragsâ, marked â) is the sound that begins English words such as is, and, action, and over, but unlike English it occurs at the end of Tagalog words: katagâ, pasô, biglâ, maiklî, pakô, malî, punô. The mild glottal stop (malumi, marked à) is a real phoneme that tells apart words spelled the same: baga (ember) and bagà (lungs); suka (vomit) and sukà (vinegar); sala (fault, crime, sin) and salà (sieve); bata (bath robe) and batà (child). The marks are used here only to show the stop, not in ordinary spelling; the first column is what is spoken.

When two or more vowel sounds come one after the other, each vowel is pronounced as a distinct unit, and there are no silent letters. Stress is shown in the syllabication: paa (pa-á), taon (ta-ón), daan (da-án), saan (sa-án), leeg (le-ég), poon (po-ón), mabait (ma-ba-ít), doon (do-ón), maalat (ma-á-lat), mataas (ma-ta-ás), kailan (ka-i-lán), maaari (ma-a-á-ri), look (lo-ók).

lessons.title: 3. C1 L1 · Consonants that need practice
lessons.subtitle: k, p, t · r · t, d, n, s · ng · l · minimal pairs

explanations.title: K, p and t are not aspirated
explanations.body: In Tagalog /k/, /p/ and /t/ are not aspirated: there is no puff of air after them. To hear the difference say kill and skill: /k/ is aspirated in kill but not in skill (and likewise pill and spill, till and still). Aspirating them does not change the meaning but gives a foreign accent.

explanations.title: The Tagalog r
explanations.body: The Tagalog /r/ is made by quickly tapping the tongue against the gum ridge, not by curling it back as in English. Mispronouncing it does not change the meaning but affects the clarity.

explanations.title: T, d, n and s
explanations.body: The consonants /t/, /d/, /n/ and /s/ are pronounced with the tip of the tongue at the back of the upper teeth; in English they are made behind the upper gum ridge.

rows: maid of honor; game of checkers

explanations.title: Minimal pairs
explanations.body: The book pairs letters that are easily confused: p/b, t/d, k/g, s/h, m/n, n/ng, n/l, d/r, l/r and w/y.

explanations.title: The consonant ng
explanations.body: Tagalog /ng/ is like the sound in singing, ringing, belonging, but it begins words (ngayon), which never happens in English; try saying si-nging, ri-nging, then si-ng along. American learners tend to substitute /n/ for it at the beginning of a word, so practice the pairs below. In writing, the sequence ng followed by g is written ngg and pronounced as in bingo.

rows: animal’s burrow or hole in the ground

explanations.title: The Tagalog l
explanations.body: In English /l/ is made with the tip of the tongue somewhere along the roof of the mouth, leaving the sides open. In Tagalog the tongue is flat from the tip to the back, with the tip at the back of the upper teeth.

lessons.title: 5. C1 L1 · A brief history of the Filipino language
lessons.subtitle: Spanish period · the rebellion · from Tagalog to Pilipino to Filipino · fiestas

explanations.title: The video script, in brief
explanations.body: The book gives the script of a three-part video, A Brief History of the Filipino Language. The summaries below are mine.

rows: When the Spaniards claimed the Philippines in the 16th century it was not a unified nation and shared no common language: about 7,000 islands, and many had their own languages (on Luzon alone, Ilocano, Tagalog and Bicol, among others).

Spanish missionaries wanted Filipinos to learn Spanish, but the church and the government in Spain did not want a repeat of the abuses in Mexico, where people who failed to learn Spanish were severely punished. So the missionaries took a gentler approach: they learned and documented the native languages themselves. This worked well and the natives embraced Roman Catholicism, but it also meant the country was never united under one language; even the American and Japanese occupations could not change that, and today about 120 languages divide the country.

Proficiency in Spanish was required for government, church or business employment, but there was no mandatory education in Spanish, so very few Filipinos qualified and leadership stayed a Spanish monopoly. By the end of the 19th century more Filipinos had mastered Spanish, yet the Spaniards kept the higher positions for themselves; some Filipinos who demanded parity were persecuted or martyred, and the resentment led to a nationwide rebellion.

The rebellion grew into a revolution to form a national Filipino government, and the rebels proclaimed independence from Spain in Kawit, Cavite, on June 12, 1898. At first Spanish was the official language of the revolution: the national anthem and the declaration of independence were written in Spanish. But some believed the national language should be based on the people’s own language, such as Tagalog; seven of the eight original provinces of the revolution (Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Manila, Cavite, Laguna and Batangas) were Tagalog-speaking, and the eighth, Pampanga, understood Tagalog. The wish for a national language climaxed in World War II, when Filipinos, after Spanish and English, were forced to learn Japanese.
Post-war: from Tagalog to Filipino (Segment C)

After the war all schools had to teach a nationalized version of Tagalog, called Pilipino from 1959. The Institute of National Language (Surian ng Wikang Pambansa) had to unify regional differences: in Bicol “Nakain ka ba ng isda?” means “Do you eat fish?”, but in Manila it means “Were you eaten by a fish?”; Batangas says “Maganda siya, eh” where Bulacan says “Siya ay maganda”; and in Pampanga the H drops from words (bahay becomes baay) and is added to others (mataas becomes matahas). From the 1940s to the 1980s the effort succeeded and most Filipinos came to speak nationalized Tagalog or Pilipino.
Post-war: from Tagalog to Filipino (Segment C)

In the late 1980s there were efforts to call Pilipino by another name, Filipino. The 1987 Constitution identifies Filipino and English as the two official languages. Filipino is not simply Pilipino renamed: it is meant to take in words from other Philippine languages such as Cebuano (spoken by 20 million) and Ilocano (11 million), and the University of the Philippines published the UP Diksyonaryong Filipino. Over the last 30 years Filipino has continued to replace Tagalog and Pilipino as the name of the national language.

explanations.title: Culture note: fiestas
explanations.body: Fiestas are part of Philippine culture and must go on through good times and bad. Every city, town, barrio and barangay has at least one local festival of its own, usually on the feast of its patron saint, so on any given day there is a fiesta somewhere in the country. Hospitality is best shown during these fiestas: anyone, including a stranger passing by, is welcome to share the food, and no invitation is required. A fiesta is celebrated in the local language, not in Spanish or English.

explanations.title: Timelines (Activity 26, my summary)
explanations.body: 1959: nationalized Tagalog becomes Pilipino and is taught in all schools. 1940s to 1980s: the Institute of National Language unifies regional differences; Pilipino becomes useful in legal, commercial and military affairs, and most Filipinos come to speak it. 1987: the Constitution names Filipino and English as the official languages; Filipino is meant to include words from other Philippine languages; the University of the Philippines publishes a Filipino dictionary.

explanations.title: The Philippines in a note
explanations.body: The Republic of the Philippines is a sovereign state in archipelagic Southeast Asia, with 7,600 islands (the introduction says 7,107) spanning more than 300,000 square kilometers. It was named after Prince Philip (later King Philip II) of Spain by the explorer Ruy Lopez de Villalobos during his 1542 to 1546 expedition. As of March 31, 2017 there are 18 regions, 81 provinces, 145 cities and 1,489 municipalities. The map in the book is for reference only.

explanations.title: The five vowels
explanations.body: The book gives approximate English sounds: a (altitude, father, summer), e (emphatic, met, inset), i (sit, bit, hit), o (soul, solitude, oblivious), u (ultimate, boomerang, optimum). In phrase-final position /o/ varies freely with /u/ (sinu-sino) and /e/ with /i/, but they are separate sounds because they distinguish meaning in some words. The mid vowels /e/ and /o/ are fairly new sounds taken from Spanish.

explanations.title: e versus i, o versus u

explanations.title: Diphthongs
explanations.body: Diphthongs combine vowel and semi-vowel sounds: /iw/, /ey/, /ay/, /aw/, /oy/ and /uy/. Except /iw/ and /uy/, all have English counterparts (ey as in say, hey, weigh; ay as in ride, lie, my; aw as in house, bow, aloud; oy as in deploy, loiter, soil). The diphthong /iw/ at the end of a word is hard for English speakers, who split it into more syllables: sisiw (chick) must not become sisiyew.

explanations.title: Days of the week (mga araw ng linggo)

explanations.title: Two sets of numbers
explanations.body: Tagalog uses two sets of numbers. One is native Tagalog, from Malay, and is normally used for counting objects, people and money, and with weights and heights. The other is derived from Spanish and is used for telling time, addresses, telephone numbers and occasionally prices. Many Filipinos use a mixture of the two.

explanations.title: Numbers in context
explanations.body: Ilan asks “how many”. The linkers ng (after a vowel, written g after the vowel) and na join a number to what it counts: anim na talampakan (six feet), dalawang dali (two inches). For dates, add a- (with the hyphen) before the Spanish derivative number: a-uno ng Mayo; the exception is 14, katorse, which does not take a-. The phone number is read digit by digit in the Spanish derivative numbers. After the number of siblings you may add lang or lang po (only).

explanations.title: Facts and figures (Activity 20a, the book’s key)
explanations.body: Review of the Introduction to the Tagalog Language and Culture:

rows: The Philippines is an archipelago of about 7,107 islands divided into 70 provinces that cover 17 regions.
Tagalog is used as a second language by over 60 million people, out of a population of approximately 94 million.
The Philippines was under American rule for 48 years and Spanish rule for 280 years.
The Philippines has a high literacy rate, and 92.6% of persons over 15 can read and write.
Although Philippine society is patriarchal, women have had a high status since pre-Hispanic times.
Muslims in the Philippines are mainly concentrated in Luzon.
Religion is central to the lives of most Filipinos, and they openly express their faith.

explanations.title: Three cultural traits (Activity 20b, from the introduction)
explanations.body: Utang na loob (debt of gratitude): a person acknowledges a debt of gratitude to someone who did a favor, saved their life or helped them in any way, and will repay the good deed in any way. Bayanihan (from bayani, “hero”): a cooperative spirit for the good of everyone; for example, if one family needs to repair their house, all the neighbors help. Mano po: a traditional sign of respect, particularly for parents, grandparents, godparents, aunts and uncles; the person says the phrase while putting the elder’s right hand to their forehead, on coming home from school, work or church, after the six o’clock evening prayer bells, or when introduced to another’s parent or other elders.

explanations.body: Five short videos in Tagalog:

Courtship (video): the four stages are the teasing phase, the human bridge, the serious stage and telling the parents; parents play two roles, interrogating the suitor and giving permission to date their daughter. Balut egg (video): the participants of the reality show Fear Factor were grossed out or disgusted and some vomited; the book’s three descriptions of balut are colorful, a potent aphrodisiac, and delicious.

explanations.title: Review: classroom expressions (Activity 1)
explanations.body: The book plays seven expressions and asks you to number them in the order you hear them; here they are for reading aloud.

rows: Please say it louder, sir/ma’am (to more than one person or out of respect).

explanations.title: Tagalog numbers 11 to 20
explanations.body: Learning the first nine numbers helps you understand the higher ones. Eleven to nineteen are labi- plus a linker plus the number: the linker is -ng after a vowel-ending prefix before a vowel (labing-isa), -n before d, l, s, t (labindalawa, labintatlo, labinlima, labinsiyam) and -m before p or b (labimpito). Twenty is dalawa + m + pu. The linkers are taught in detail in Chapter 3.

explanations.title: Telling the time in Tagalog (Activity 2a)
explanations.body: Write ika- (with a hyphen) before the number: ika-labing-isa ng umaga is eleven in the morning. Ika- also makes ordinal numbers (taught in Chapter 2). Exceptions: ikalawa (2:00) drops the da of dalawa and ikatlo (3:00) drops the ta of tatlo. Do not mix Tagalog and Spanish numbers: ika-nuwebe is wrong.

rows: 2:00 (ika-2); the da of dalawa is dropped
3:00 (ika-3); the ta of tatlo is dropped

examples.translation: Celia: Dino, what time is it now?
Dino: It’s eleven in the morning.

explanations.title: Saying your age (Activity 2b)
explanations.body: The short answer gives only the number; the long answer adds taong gulang (years old). Na is an enclitic particle with many uses; here it means “now” or “already”: Ilang taong gulang ka na? is “How old are you (now)?”. The linker ng joins the number to taong gulang: Tatlumpu’t dalawang taong gulang na. Use po or ho to higher-ranking classmates.

rows: How old are you? (literally: What is your age?)
Ikaw, ano na ang edad mo?

explanations.title: Four kinds of stress
explanations.body: Stress is important in Tagalog because it sometimes changes the meaning of the word altogether. Tagalog words are generally pronounced as they are spelled, but the glottal stop is not shown in ordinary spelling; the marks below are used in teaching materials. A glottal stop is made by tightly closing the glottis, the opening between the vocal cords; English has one in “uh-oh”. In Tagalog it occurs in final position, and sometimes in initial position.

rows: Stress on the final syllable, with a glottal stop
Penultimate stress with a glottal catch

explanations.title: Glottal stops at the beginning, middle and end (Activity 7)
explanations.body: End stress: lumpó, kakaibá. Penultimate stress: lumo, umaga. A glottal stop in initial position: àbala, ìkaw, àko. A glottal stop in final position: tamà.

explanations.title: The glottal stop in fast speech (Activity 8)

explanations.title: Tens in Tagalog
explanations.body: Each ten is built from the first nine numbers plus a linker plus pu (ten): -m after a vowel before p, na after a consonant. The final o of tatlo, pito and walo changes to u (tatlumpu, pitumpu, walumpu). One hundred is isa + n + daan.

explanations.title: Putting the tens and ones together
explanations.body: For the twenties, thirties and so on, add each of the first nine numbers with ’t, the contracted at (and): Tagalog literally says “twenty and one”. The final n of isandaan drops before ’t (isandaa’t isa); this is also true of dalawandaan (200). Native speakers tend to drop the i of isandaan in speech (sandaan).

explanations.title: Practice table (Activity 10, completed)

explanations.title: Hundreds in Tagalog
explanations.body: Add each of the first nine numbers to a hundred in the same way as before (’t or at joins the rest): the n of daan drops before ’t. An o changes to u when a syllable or the linker ng follows (tatlundaan, pitundaan, walundaan), and the g of the linker ng drops before d (limandaan, pitundaan, walundaan); later you will learn other letters that cause the g to drop.

explanations.title: Hundreds in the Spanish derivative

explanations.title: Area and distance (Activities 22, 23, 25, 26)
explanations.body: The metric system is used in the Philippines, although some establishments still use the old imperial system. Ano ang sukat ng …? asks the area (in metro kuwadrado); Gaano kalayo ang …? asks how far (in kilometro, or milya for miles). The long answer ends with ang sukat ng … or ang layo ng …. The first two models use Tagalog numbers, the second two the Spanish derivative.

explanations.title: Thousands
explanations.body: Tagalog: isa + n + libo; dalawa + n + libo, and ’t joins the rest (isanlibo’t limandaan). Spanish derivative: mil, dos mil, mil kinyentos, dos mil diyes.

explanations.title: Dates of birth in Tagalog (Activity 27)
explanations.body: Anong petsa ka ipinanganak? literally asks “What date were you born?”. Noong means “on” or “in” a past time. Dates use ika- plus a Tagalog number (ika-dalawampu ng Marso, ika-labing-isa ng Mayo); the year follows taong. The long answer ends with ako ipinanganak.

examples.translation: Lira: Zen, what’s your date of birth? (literally: what date were you born?)

examples.text: Noong ika-dalawampu ng Marso, taong isanlibo’t siyamnaraa’t siyamnapu’t siyam.
examples.translation: Zen: On the twentieth of March, the year 1999. (short answer)
Zen: You, what is your date of birth?

examples.text: Noong ika-labing-isa ng Mayo, taong isanlibo’t siyamnaraa’t walumpu’t walo.
examples.translation: Lira: On the eleventh of May, the year 1988.

examples.text: Noong ika-dalawampu ng Marso, taong isanlibo’t siyamnaraa’t siyamnapu’t siyam ako ipinanganak.
examples.translation: Zen: I was born on the twentieth of March, 1999. (long answer)

examples.text: Noong ika-labing-isa ng Mayo, taong isanlibo’t siyamnaraa’t walumpu’t walo ako ipinanganak.
examples.translation: Lira: I was born on the eleventh of May, 1988.

explanations.title: Dates of birth in Spanish (Activity 28)
explanations.body: Kailan ka ipinanganak? asks “When were you born?”. Spanish derivative dates take a-: a-trese ng Abril, a-beynte singko ng Disyembre. Years are read as mil + hundreds + the rest: mil nuwebe siyentos otsenta (1980).

examples.translation: Liz: Leo, when were you born?

examples.text: Noong a-trese ng Abril, mil nuwebe siyentos otsenta.
examples.translation: Leo: On the thirteenth of April, 1980. (short answer)

examples.translation: Leo: I was born on the thirteenth of April, 1980. (long answer)

explanations.body: The glossary of Days 1 to 3 repeats these questions and answers; in the blanks of the book you supply the number or the date.

explanations.title: Bingo and the national anthem (Activity 29)
explanations.body: Activity 29 is a bingo game with the teacher calling a letter and number (for example I-2); the winner calls out “Bingo! Panalo po ako” (Bingo! I’m a winner, sir/ma’am). The day ends with the Philippine national anthem, Lupang Hinirang, read aloud for practice of the vowels, consonants and diphthongs and then sung with the song. The lyrics are not copied here; read them in your book. Some words from it that you can already use: bayan, perlas, dagat, bundok, langit, bituin, araw, watawat.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation (Chapter 1, Days 1 to 3)
explanations.body: After the three introductory days the book asks you to check that you can say the alphabet, pronounce the difficult sounds, associate sounds with letters, recognize Spanish and English cognates, use classroom expressions, greet people formally and informally, introduce yourself briefly, count in Tagalog and Spanish from 1 to 10, use leave-taking expressions, ask the days and months, ask for and state time, age and date of birth, name colors and shapes, and that you understand the history of the Filipino language, Filipino names and places, and Filipino tradition and culture. If not, review the section, find a study partner, or ask your academic counselor for help.

explanations.title: Getting started
explanations.body: Greet your classmates and introduce yourself: your rank, name and place of origin, with honorifics as appropriate. Model: Magandang araw (or umaga, hapon, tanghali). Ako si ____. Taga-____ ako.

explanations.title: Presentation A: introducing oneself and others
explanations.body: Ako and siya are singular personal pronouns; ito means “this”. Si goes before one person’s name, sina before two or more names. Ay works like the verb “to be” (am, is, are, was) and is often left out in conversation. Mga makes a noun plural and is said ma-nga.

examples.text: Ako si Daniel. Ako ay Amerikano.
examples.translation: I am Daniel. I am an American.

examples.text: Siya si Bing. Siya ay Pilipino.
examples.translation: She (or he) is Bing. Bing is a Filipino.

examples.text: Ito sina Maring at Ging-Ging. Sina Maring at Ging-Ging ay mga Pilipino rin.
examples.translation: These are Maring and Ging-Ging. Maring and Ging-Ging are also Filipinos.

examples.text: Siya si Hans. Si Hans ay Aleman.
examples.translation: He is Hans. Hans is a German.

examples.text: Siya si Rong. Si Rong ay Intsik.
examples.translation: He is Rong. Rong is a Chinese.

explanations.title: Culture note: nicknames
explanations.body: When people are familiar with each other, many Filipinos use nicknames, many of which end in -ing: Marina becomes Maring, Pedro becomes Pedring. Some nicknames repeat the first syllable of the person’s name (Jojo, Mai-Mai, Ging-Ging). Younger children are affectionately called Nene, Girlie, Boy or Boyet, and these names are often carried into adulthood.

explanations.title: Who is what? (Comprehension checks 1 and 2, the book’s key)
explanations.body: Names and their nationalities from Presentation A, and names with occupations from Presentation B (the next lesson).

explanations.title: Set I markers
explanations.body: Markers are essential parts of the Tagalog sentence. They mark or signal the focus, or topic, of the sentence and have no equivalents in English. There are three groups: the Set I (ang) markers taught here, and the ng and sa markers taught later. Focus is the point of emphasis of the sentence; in English definiteness is sometimes shown by “the”, or by tone and heavier stress. Iyong (shortened to ’yung) is a pronominal adjective often used in conversation in place of ang. Proper nouns (Lucy, Microsoft) are capitalized; common nouns (boy, car) name general things.

explanations.title: Dialog 1 (a singular name)
explanations.body: A question with sino can be answered in three ways: with the predicate alone (marked by ang), with the predicate first, or with the topic first. Every answer uses Set I markers in both the topic and the predicate, so the predicate is made definite.

lessons.title: 24. C1 L4 · The Tagalog sentence: ay and predicate first
lessons.subtitle: Si Rong ay Intsik. · Intsik si Rong. · Subject + ay + predicate · Predicate + subject

explanations.title: Two word orders
explanations.body: The Tagalog sentence has two distinct word orders: subject + predicate (S-P) and predicate + subject (P-S). The S-P order is sometimes called the “ay construction”; it is less common in conversation and more common in writing. The word-for-word translation of Ako ay Amerikano is “I American”.

rows: Sina Maring at Ging-Ging ay mga Pilipino rin.
Maring and Ging-Ging are also Filipino.

explanations.title: Subject + ay + predicate
explanations.body: Ay seems to behave like the English “to be”, but unlike the verb “to be” it only joins a subject and a predicate in this order. The pattern is: marker + noun phrase + ay + complement (a noun phrase or an adjective), for example Si Rong ay Intsik. Si and sina have no English equivalent. The subject + predicate order is rarely used in conversational Tagalog.

explanations.title: Predicate + subject
explanations.body: This is the order commonly used in conversation. Ay is not used. The same sentences can be restated by putting the predicate first; the English translation is the same, but the word order is reversed.

rows: Mga Pilipino rin sina Maring at Ging-Ging.
Maring and Ging-Ging are also Filipino.

explanations.title: Culture note: mano po and hospitality
explanations.body: Mano po (literally “your hand, sir/ma’am”) is a traditional sign of respect. You say it while putting an elder’s right hand to your forehead. The response is Kaawaan ka ng Diyos (literally “May God have mercy on you”, which in this context means “God bless you”). Filipinos are gracious hosts and are known for their hospitality; inviting visitors to eat is normal, as the mother does here.

explanations.title: Notes
explanations.body: Halikayo is a contraction of halika (come) and kayo (you). Halikayo, kain tayo means “Come, let’s eat.” Kayo means “you, plural” when Pia’s friend is spoken to (Kumusta kayo?) and “you, singular polite” when the mother is spoken to (Kamusta po kayo?).

explanations.title: Culture note: Ano’ng atin? and Saan ang lakad?
explanations.body: A common greeting in Tagalog is Ano’ng atin? or Saan ang lakad? (or Saan ka pupunta? or Saan ang punta?), meaning “What’s up? Where are you going?”. It is an informal greeting equivalent to “Hello” or “Hi” and is not meant to find out information. A vague Diyan lang (contracted D’yan lang, “Just there”), Wala lang (“Nothing, really”), a smile or a raising of the eyebrows to acknowledge the greeting is often enough of an answer.

explanations.title: Leave-taking expressions

lessons.title: 28. C1 L5 · Set I personal pronouns

explanations.title: The pronouns
explanations.body: A pronoun substitutes for a noun. Set I pronouns are distinguished by person (first, second, third) and by number.

rows: we (exclusive: does not include the person spoken to)
we (inclusive: includes the person spoken to)

explanations.title: Using the pronouns in sentences
explanations.body: Any pronoun can replace the subject: Ako ay Amerikano becomes Ikaw ay Amerikano, Siya ay Amerikano, Kami ay Amerikano, Tayo ay Amerikano, Kayo ay Amerikano or Sila ay Amerikano. In the predicate + subject order, which is common in conversation, you say Amerikano ako, Amerikano ka, Amerikano siya, Amerikano kami, Amerikano tayo, Amerikano kayo, Amerikano sila.

rows: He or she is an American.

explanations.title: Rule 1: ka and ikaw
explanations.body: There are two forms of “you, singular”. Ka is never used to start a sentence, while ikaw can. It is wrong to say Ka Amerikano; say Amerikano ka. Ikaw can stand alone as a short answer, but ka cannot: Sino ang Amerikano? Ikaw.

explanations.title: Rule 2: kami and tayo
explanations.body: In the first person plural, “we” has two forms. Kami (exclusive) leaves out the person being spoken to; tayo (inclusive) includes that person. In Passage A, Liz says Ayos lang kami (we are fine: herself and her friends, excluding the mother), and the mother says Halikayo, kumain tayo (come, let’s eat: herself, Liz and her friends).

explanations.title: Rule 3: siya and sila
explanations.body: Siya is a genderless pronoun and may refer to a man or a woman. Sila means “they” (third person plural), and it may also be singular and polite: on the telephone a receptionist often asks a client Sino po sila? (literally “Who are they?”) to be courteous. In Passage A, sila refers to the plural “they”.

explanations.title: Set I demonstrative pronouns
explanations.body: Demonstrative pronouns (“this”, “that”) sometimes replace nouns and pronouns. There are three sets of demonstratives in Tagalog; this lesson covers Set I, focusing on people (in Tagalog it is very common to use demonstratives to stand for people).

explanations.title: Passage C: sino with demonstratives
explanations.body: Tanong means “question” and sagot means “answer”.

explanations.title: Structures
explanations.body: The question: Sino + Set I demonstrative pronoun. The response: noun + Set I demonstrative pronoun. In the book’s examples the book writes the plural ang mga in brackets: Sino (ang mga) iyon? Mga guro (ang mga) iyon., so the short forms Sino iyon? and Mga guro iyon. are also used.

explanations.body: A model of the pair work: you introduce your friends to your teacher with the right courtesy, using Bb. (Binibini), G. (Ginoo) or Gng. (Ginang) before the name; with a single friend, use the single pronoun and si instead of sina. Switch roles and let your teacher give feedback (the pair work is left out; a model dialog is below).

explanations.title: Greetings, courtesies and leave-taking (the glossary table)
explanations.body: Greetings: Kamusta po kayo? (How are you, sir/ma’am?), Ano’ng atin? (What’s up?), Saan ang lakad? (Where are you going?). Leave-taking: O, sige (impliedly saying goodbye), Hanggang sa susunod (until next time), Hanggang sa isang linggo (until next week). explanations.title: Getting started

explanations.title: Presentation 1: Patricia introduces her family
explanations.body: Patricia, an American college student, introduces her family. Notes: Ito (this) is a demonstrative pronoun referring to her family; namin (our, exclusive) refers only to Patricia and her family, not to the listener; magkakapatid comes from the root kapatid (sibling); pangalawa, pangatlo and pang-apat are ordinal numbers (see lesson 4).

explanations.title: Presentation 2: introducing family members
explanations.body: The seventeen expressions of the book. Si and sina have no English equivalent; siya and sila are the Set I pronouns. Pinsan, pamangkin, apo, manugang, asawa, anak and biyenan can be a man or a woman; add babae (girl) or lalaki (boy) to be specific: pamangking babae is “niece” and pamangking lalaki is “nephew”. The g in pamangking is a linker.

explanations.title: Hipag, bayaw and bilas
explanations.body: The hipag is one’s spouse’s sister or one’s sister-in-law. The bayaw is one’s spouse’s brother or brother-in-law. The spouse, male or female, of one’s hipag or bayaw is called bilas.

explanations.title: The Set II pronouns
explanations.body: The pronouns are distinguished by person and number. The structure of a possessive phrase is: ang (or ang mga) + noun + Set II pronoun.

explanations.title: Ordinal numbers, first to tenth
explanations.body: Except for una, ordinal numbers are built with pang-, pan- or pam- before the number: dalawa becomes pangalawa (the d drops) and tatlo becomes pangatlo (the t drops). The numbers 1 to 10 you already know are isa, dalawa, tatlo, apat, lima, anim, pito, walo, siyam and sampu.

lessons.title: 36. C2 L2 · Set II possessive markers: ni, nina, ng, ng mga
lessons.subtitle: ang kuya ni Jobert · ang nanay nina Bambam at Noynoy · ang bahay ng mga titser · Ano ang …?

explanations.title: Passage C: sentences with ni, nina, ng and ng mga
explanations.body: The predicates of these sentences are nouns, pronouns or adjectives; such sentences are called equational sentences. In English the predicate and the subject are joined by the linking verb “to be”, but Tagalog has no “to be” linking verb. Matangkad, maganda, mabait, matalino, maliit, malinis, malaki and masikip are ma adjectives.

examples.translation: Jingjing and Bobot’s uncle is intelligent.

examples.text: Malaki ang bahay ng mga titser.
Masikip ang opisina ng mga titser.

explanations.title: The Set II possessive markers
explanations.body: Like the Set II pronouns, the Set II markers come before the noun they modify. They translate as “of” or “’s” (and sometimes “s’”). They also mark the noun that does the action in some sentences where the focus is on the object, which you will see with the verbs.

rows: names of two or more persons

explanations.title: Translations of the book’s sentences
explanations.body: Each sentence can be translated in two ways: Jobert’s oldest brother is tall, or The oldest brother of Jobert is tall.

explanations.title: The interrogative ano
explanations.body: Ano means “what”. It usually refers to things, but it is also used with people when the expected answers are professions (rank, title), gender, status (marital, immigration, social), religion or nationality.

explanations.title: Ma adjectives
explanations.body: Tagalog adjectives are of two kinds by structure: simple adjectives (root words) and ma adjectives (ma + root word). The structure of an equational sentence with them is adjective + noun + Set II marker + noun. The book asks you to find four more ma adjectives in a dictionary.

explanations.title: Listening exchanges (Activity 4, the book’s script)
explanations.body: The chart asks for nationality, religion and adjective. Key in short: (1) Gracia Italian, George British; (2) Soledad Protestant; (3) the teachers are intelligent, Filipino and Catholic; (4) Jose Spanish, Jorge German, Adrian Greek, Jack and Oliver Australian; (5) the classroom is big and clean, the students Indonesian, Chinese, Japanese and Vietnamese; (6) Carolina’s cousins are Jehovah’s Witnesses and Carolina is Iglesia ni Kristo. You may hear the fillers eh and ah, which are common in ordinary conversation.

examples.text: Italyano si Gracia. Eh, si George, ano ang nasyonalidad niya?
examples.translation: Gracia is Italian. And George, what is his nationality?

examples.text: Mga classmates ko po. Sina Jose, Jorge, Adrian, Jack, at Oliver.
examples.translation: My classmates, sir/ma’am. Jose, Jorge, Adrian, Jack and Oliver.

examples.text: Espanyol si Jose. Aleman naman si Jorge. Griyego si Adrian, at Australyano sina Jack at Oliver.
examples.translation: Jose is Spanish. Jorge is German. Adrian is Greek, and Jack and Oliver are Australian.

examples.text: Malaki at malinis ang silid-aralan ng mga sundalo. Ano ang mga nasyonalidad ng mga estudyante dito?
examples.translation: The soldiers’ classroom is big and clean. What are the nationalities of the students here?

examples.text: Mga Indones, Intsik, Hapon, at Biyetnamis.
Mga Saksi ni Jehovah ang mga pinsan ni Carolina.
Eh, si Carolina, ano ang relihiyon niya?
examples.translation: And Carolina, what is her religion?

examples.text: Iglesia ni Kristo ang relihiyon ni Carolina.
examples.translation: Carolina’s religion is the Iglesia ni Kristo.

explanations.title: Facebook friends (Activity 5, the book’s script and key)
explanations.body: Key: the nationalities of the man’s friends are Spanish, Australian and Arab; they are tall, intelligent and nice; the women are the man’s teachers, described by nationality and religion (Americans and Protestants); the last person asked about is the little child, the man’s niece or nephew, the child of his cousin.

examples.text: Ito ang mga kaibigan ko. Ito sina Angelo, Roger, at Hasheed. Espanyol si Angelo, Australyano si Roger, at Arabe si Hasheed.
examples.translation: Man: These are my friends. These are Angelo, Roger and Hasheed. Angelo is Spanish, Roger is Australian and Hasheed is Arab.
Woman: They are tall, aren’t they.

examples.text: Sila ang mga titser ko. Mga Amerikano at Protestante sila.
examples.translation: Man: They are my teachers. They are Americans and Protestants.
Woman: Who is this small child?

examples.text: Pamangkin ko siya. Anak siya ng pinsan ko.
examples.translation: Man: He or she is my niece or nephew. He or she is my cousin’s child.

explanations.title: Asking details about a person (Speaking, Activity 6: the model)
explanations.body: Ask a partner about nationality, religion, age, weight and height. It is preferable to say sentences without ay, since ay is more common in formal conversation or in specific Tagalog regions in Luzon, but you can use ay for practice. Talampakan and dali are feet and inches; piye and pulgada are the Spanish-derived words.

examples.text: Ilang taong gulang na si John?
Anim na talampakan at dalawang dali.
Ang taas ni John ay sais piye at dos pulgada.
examples.translation: John’s height is six feet two inches.

explanations.title: Introducing a person (Activity 7: the two models)
explanations.body: Introduce each person in a list to a classmate, adding courtesies and honorifics and ending with a leave-taking expression.

examples.text: Siya si John. Amerikano siya. Mormon ang relihiyon niya. Estudyante siya dito. Labinsiyam na taong gulang siya.
examples.translation: This is John. He is American. His religion is Mormon. He is a student here. He is nineteen years old.

examples.text: Ito si John. Siya ay Amerikano. Mormon siya. Siya ay estudyante. Disinuwebe anyos siya.
examples.translation: This is John. He is an American. He is Mormon. He is a student. He is nineteen years old. (Native speakers tend to use this model.)

explanations.title: Taga-saan
explanations.body: Filipinos often ask “Where are you from?” when they meet for the first time: Taga-saan ka? The speaker and the answerer have in mind the place of birth or the place of origin that the person considers home, usually a town, city or province, not a country. The expected answer is Taga- + place. Taga-saan and Taga- + place can only be used for people, never for things or animals.

lessons.title: 39. C2 L3 · The particle ba, confirmation questions and tag questions
lessons.subtitle: Taga-Ohio ba si Lucia? · Hindi ba inhinyero si Jason? · Medyor si Simon, hindi ba? · ano?

explanations.title: The enclitic particle ba
explanations.body: Yes/no questions in Tagalog use the enclitic particle ba. Enclitic particles are one- and two-syllable words (like naman) that normally come after the first full word of the sentence. Ba signals a yes/no question and has no English equivalent. It is usually left out when an interrogative like “who”, “what” or “when” is already in the sentence, but it can be used with these to make a question more emphatic or to clarify a response. A question can be answered with a short “yes” or “no” or with a full sentence.

examples.text: Hindi. Hindi taga-Ohio si Lucia. Taga-Kansas siya.
examples.translation: No. Lucia is not from Ohio. She is from Kansas.
Simon is a major, isn’t he?
Simon is a major, isn’t he?
No. Simon is not a major.
No. He is not a major.

explanations.title: Confirmation questions
explanations.body: The English question “Isn’t Celso a doctor?” is Hindi ba doktor si Celso?

examples.translation: Yes. He is. (answer 1 in the book’s example about Jason)

examples.text: Hindi. Hindi siya inhinyero. Kusinero siya.
examples.translation: No. He is not an engineer. He is a cook.

explanations.title: Tag questions
explanations.body: There are only two question tags in Tagalog, and they are easier than the English ones: ano? and hindi ba?. They alternate freely and do not depend on the phrase before them, unlike English, where the tag reflects the tense and a negative phrase gets an affirmative tag.

examples.translation: He is not a major, is he?
He is not a major, is he?
Yes, sir/ma’am. He is not a major. (agreeing with the statement)
No, sir/ma’am. He is a major. (disagreeing, because he is in fact a major)

explanations.title: Note on agreeing and disagreeing
explanations.body: In the last example, Opo. Hindi siya medyor means the person agrees with the statement that he is not a major; Hindi. Medyor po siya means the person disagrees, because he is in fact a major. English speakers must get used to this: it is the opposite of their usual answers to such questions (Oo agrees with the content of the statement; Hindi contradicts it).

explanations.body: The endings -era and -ero show the Spanish influence on Tagalog. A noun in this category names a person with a certain occupation: -era is a woman and -ero a man. Some words take both, others only one. Some jobs are associated with men (a tubero, plumber, is usually a man’s job in the Philippines), others with women (a labandera, a woman who does laundry for a living). Exceptions: dispatsador (salesman), doktor and propesor end in -or, not -ero.

explanations.title: Usually only male or only female
explanations.body: You may add more -era nouns when you find them.

explanations.title: Presentation 2: Romeo describes his stepmother
explanations.body: Paki- in pakilarawan means “please”. Bewang is how baywang (waistline) is often pronounced. Malapad, malaki, mataba, makapal, maputi, maiksi and maitim are ma adjectives; pandak, kayumanggi, bilugan, itim, kulot, singkit, kulay itim, pango and bilog are simple (non-ma) adjectives.

explanations.title: Simple adjectives and ma adjectives
explanations.body: Adjectives are descriptive words that modify nouns. Tagalog adjectives are of two kinds by structure: simple adjectives (root words) and ma adjectives (ma + root word). To ask for a physical description say Ilarawan mo nga si ____ or Ilarawan mo nga ang ____.

examples.text: Kayumanggi ang kulay ng balat niya.
Itim at kulot ang buhok niya.

explanations.title: Ma + root word
explanations.body: Identify the root words of the ma adjectives.

explanations.title: Ma adjectives as predicate
explanations.body: Adjectives may function as the predicate of a sentence: the adjective comes first and the noun follows.

examples.text: Mahaba ang mga braso at daliri niya.
examples.translation: His arms and fingers are long.

examples.text: Manipis at mapula ang labi niya.

explanations.title: Adjectives as noun modifiers
explanations.body: Adjectives may also modify a noun or noun phrase using a linker (ng, na or g), which you will learn in detail in Chapter 3, Lesson 3. In short: ng is attached to words ending in a vowel, g to words ending in n, and na is a separate word after other consonants. The structure is adjective + linker + noun, or noun + linker + adjective. (The book also gives siko at tuhod na maitim for the last example.)

rows: Maitim ang tuhod at siko niya.

Notes: Ilan ang kapatid mo? means “How many siblings do you have?” and excludes the listener; you may also ask Ilan kayong magkakapatid? (How many siblings are there in your family?). explanations.title: The questions in the passages
explanations.body: You have already met ano (Ano ang trabaho mo?, Ano ang relihiyon mo?) and sino. Read these sixteen questions with a partner and pay attention to the question words; many of them were introduced in the introductory lessons of week one.

explanations.title: Saan and nasaan
explanations.body: There are two words for “where”. Saan asks about places or locations that are more or less fixed, and it is also used when there is a verb in the sentence (Saan ka ipinanganak? Saan ka nakatira? Saan ka lumaki?). Nasaan asks for a person or object that is not in a fixed location, and for places on a map. Names of places are marked with ang in Tagalog. Grammatically, the answer to a saan question starts with sa and the answer to a nasaan question starts with nasa, but native speakers sometimes use sa and nasa interchangeably.

rows: Where in Arizona? In Phoenix, sir/ma’am.
Where in Texas? In Houston, sir/ma’am.
Where are they now? In Arizona, sir/ma’am.
Where is your homework now? At home, sir/ma’am.
Where is the soldier? In class, sir/ma’am.
Where is Manila? Manila is in Luzon.
Where is Marawi? Marawi is in Mindanao.

examples.translation: Where in Arizona? In Phoenix, sir/ma’am.
Where in Texas? In Houston, sir/ma’am.
Where are they now? In Arizona, sir/ma’am.

explanations.title: Ilan and pang-ilan
explanations.body: Ilan means “how many” and is answered with cardinal numbers; the g in Ilang taong gulang ka na? is a linker. Pang-ilan means “which order” and is answered with ordinal numbers (the English translation depends on the context: Pang-ilan ka? asks which child you are in the family).

examples.translation: How many siblings do you have?
Which order (in the family) are you?

explanations.title: Kailan
explanations.body: Kailan means “when”. Native speakers say kelan. The structure is kailan + Set I personal pronoun + verb: Kailan ka ipinanganak? The Set I pronouns are ako, ka or ikaw, siya, kami, tayo, kayo, sila.

explanations.title: Review of ano
explanations.body: Ano means “what”. With Set II pronoun mo (possessive) the structure is below.

rows: Ano + ang + noun + Set II pronoun
Ano ang trabaho ng mga magulang mo?
Ano + ang + noun + ng mga + plural noun + Set II pronoun

explanations.title: Summary of the question words
explanations.body: The words in parentheses are how native speakers say them. The plural forms are used when a plural answer is expected.

explanations.title: Culture note: food and meals
explanations.body: Food is the basis of social life in the Philippines. There are three meals a day, with two snacks (miryenda, from the Spanish “merienda”) in between. Although there are native dishes, Philippine cuisine has not escaped foreign influences, especially Spanish. The dining table at fiestas is a United Nations of local and foreign food (American, French, Spanish and Chinese, among others) that sit alongside one another: native food and food from different countries adapted and accepted in the homes.

explanations.title: Notes
explanations.body: Adobo in adobong manok (chicken adobo) is the Spanish word for marinade; the dish, often considered the national dish of the Philippines, has Spanish origins. Pananghalian (a contraction of pagkain sa tanghalian) and tanghalian (literally lunch) can be used interchangeably. In kesong puti, kapeng barako, pritong itlog, adobong manok, kaning itim and tirang litson the ng is a linker used when the word ends in a vowel; the na in mainit na tsaa, inihaw na isda and sabaw na munggo is a linker used when the word before it ends in a consonant. The enclitic naman introduces a topic related to what was just said: Ano naman ang hapunan mo? means “And how about your dinner?”. Ano ang sa iyo? means “What’s yours?”. Baboy also means “pig” in another context.

explanations.title: Three linkers
explanations.body: There are three linkers: ng is attached to a word ending in a vowel, g is attached to a word ending in the letter n, and na follows a word ending in any other consonant. The first two are attached directly to the end of the word, while na is a separate word. The linker can be placed before or after the noun: adjective + linker + noun, or noun + linker + adjective.

lessons.title: 54. C3 L1 · Fractions and mixed numbers
lessons.subtitle: kalahati, katlo, kapat · tatlong-kapat · dalawa’t isang katlo · anim at kalahati

explanations.title: Fractions
explanations.body: The prefix ka- signifies “one over” a number: ka + number. Except for kalahati (1/2), katlo (1/3), kapat (1/4), kanim (1/6) and kapulo (1/10), the fractions are straightforward ka + number (kalima, kapito, kawalo, kasiyam). Two or more parts are said as number + linker + fraction: dalawang-katlo (2/3), tatlong-kapat (3/4), apat-kalima (4/5). You are expected to memorize these, knowing the numbers 1 to 10.

explanations.title: Mixed numbers
explanations.body: In mixed numbers ’t is added after a number ending in a vowel and at after a number ending in a consonant: dalawa’t isang katlo (2 1/3) but apat at kapat (4 1/4).

lessons.title: 56. C3 L2 · At the store: magkano, pabili, bayad and sukli
lessons.subtitle: Aling Maria, magkano po ang betsin? · Pabili po ng… · Heto ang sukli

explanations.title: Getting started
explanations.body: The book opens with a mind map of food and other consumable goods that Filipinos buy and asks you to add related concepts in Tagalog (the mind map is left out).

explanations.title: Advertisement (the book’s key for the prices)
explanations.body: The advertisement is a picture and cannot be reproduced; the book’s key lists the goods and prices in Spanish-derived and Tagalog numbers. One Spanish entry (the cabbage, “treynta’y kuwatro”, 34) does not match its Tagalog entry (tatlumpung piso, 30); the Tagalog one is used here.

examples.text: Aling Maria, magkano po ang betsin?
examples.translation: Man: Aling Maria, how much is the MSG, ma’am?

examples.text: Dalawang piso at limampung sentimo ang bawat pakete.
examples.translation: Woman: Two pesos and fifty centavos (₱2.50) each packet.

examples.text: Magkano po isang kahon ng mangga?
examples.translation: Man: How much is a box of mangoes, ma’am?
Woman: Two hundred ninety (₱290) each box.

examples.text: Magkano po ang isang gatang ng bigas?
examples.translation: Man: How much is a gatang of rice, ma’am?

examples.text: Beynte pesos lang ang isang gatang.
examples.translation: Woman: Only twenty pesos (₱20) a gatang.

examples.text: Pabili po ng dalawang betsin, tatlong kahong mangga, at limang gatang na bigas. Pabili rin po ng asin, asukal na pula, luya, at pamintang durog. Heto po ang bayad.
examples.translation: Man: I’d like to buy two MSG, three boxes of mangoes and five gatang of rice. I’d also like to buy salt, brown sugar, ginger and ground pepper. Here is my payment.

explanations.title: Culture note: titles of familial respect
explanations.body: In most places in the country, including the public market, it is common for Filipinos to address each other using titles of familial respect:

rows: woman who is older or of the same age
man who is older or of the same age
man (the noun form of mang; written mamà in the book)
child; used for both a younger man and woman

explanations.title: Notes
explanations.body: Aling in Aling Maria is a title of familial respect used before the first name of a woman; the noun form is ale. For a man, mang is used (Mang Juan); the noun form is mamà. A gatang is a wooden container with a volume equivalent to half a liter, commonly used for measuring grains at home; a few markets in remote areas still use it. Pabili is a way to ask a store clerk to sell you something or to let someone know you want to buy something: Pabili po ng dalawang betsin means “I’d like to buy two MSG, sir/ma’am.” Lang (“only”) indicates that the price of one gatang of rice is cheap or affordable. Heto po ang bayad means “Here’s my payment” and Heto ang sukli means “Here’s the change”. For prices greater than ten, Spanish derivative numbers are more commonly used.

rows: buy (a way to ask a seller for something)

explanations.title: Common questions and answers with demonstrative pronouns
explanations.body: For questions using ito and ang mga ito the responses use iyan and ang mga iyan, and the other way round. For iyon and ang mga iyon the same demonstratives are used in the response.

examples.translation: Question: How much is this, sir/ma’am?
Answer: That is two pesos, sir/ma’am.
Question: How much is that over there, sir/ma’am?
Answer: That over there is five hundred pesos, sir/ma’am.
Question: How much are these, sir/ma’am?
Answer: Those are fifteen pesos, sir/ma’am.
Question: How much are those over there, sir/ma’am?
Answer: Those over there are twenty pesos, sir/ma’am.

explanations.title: Notes
explanations.body: The enclitic naman introduces a topic related to what has just been said: Magkano naman po ang isang kilo ng longganisa? means “And how about the price of sausage per kilo?”. In Dialog A the currency (“peso”) is no longer mentioned: if it is understood (a kilo of meat does not cost centavos but pesos), the type of currency need not be said. In Dialog B, Ginebra and Tanduay are popular wines (the book’s word) and 555 and Ligo are popular sardine brands. Gas (kerosene) is sold in small quantities in many stores, especially in rural places where there is no electric power; people use it for lamps.

explanations.title: The question word magkano
explanations.body: When asking about the price of items, Filipinos use the question word magkano (“how much”) and the phrase magkakano ang mga ito (“how much is each of these”); the latter is introduced later in the semester. The response to magkano is simply the price of the item itself. Patterns: Honorific + Magkano po + ang + item, or Honorific + Magkano po + ang + quantity + linker + item; Magkano po + ang + quantity + linker + item; Magkano + naman po + ang + quantity + linker + item. (The book prints some linked forms run together, such as kahonng and taling; they are written correctly here.)

explanations.title: Speaking (Activities 10 and 11)
explanations.body: Play a customer at a public market: ask for the price of fish, sausage, eggs and pork, using honorifics and measures such as kilo, dosena, libra and piraso; then say Pabili po ng… and name the items with quantities. Guided Q and A: A asks the price of a bundle of moringa and a kilo of potatoes; B says the price; A asks the price of a box of mangoes and a box of apples; B says the price; A says he wants to buy three bundles of moringa, five and a half kilos of potatoes, two boxes of mangoes and a box of apples, plus salt, soy sauce, vinegar, brown and white sugar, ground and whole pepper and ginger. Use both Tagalog and Spanish-derived numbers for the prices.

explanations.title: Getting started
explanations.body: The book opens with a mind map about descriptions of food and asks you to add as many Tagalog adjectives as you can (the mind map is left out).

examples.text: Bigyan ninyo nga po ako ng isang order ng inihaw na baboy, dalawang kanin, sabaw, at buko juice.
examples.translation: Man: Will you please give me one order of grilled pork, two rice, soup and buko juice.

explanations.title: Culture note: turo-turo eateries
explanations.body: Turo-turo eateries are traditionally small, Filipino-style fast-food restaurants. They are literally everywhere. Turo-turo literally means “point-point” because you just point at the foods you want when you order them. They offer modest prices for a full meal. At present there are modern and upscale turo-turo eateries in metropolitan cities such as Manila, Cebu and Davao.

explanations.title: Notes
explanations.body: Papaitan is a popular Ilocano soup dish composed mainly of cow or goat innards; the name comes from the Filipino word pait, “bitter”. Malinamnam, masarap and malasa are synonyms, and ulam and putahe are also synonyms. In the dialog the enclitic naman introduces a related topic: Magkano naman ang sabaw? means “And how about the soup, how much is it?”. The enclitic nga means “please”: Bigyan ninyo nga po ako ng isang order ng… means “Will you please/kindly give me one order of…”. Other uses of nga will be discussed in future lessons. Pa-order naman po ng isang inihaw na baboy, dalawang kanin, at buko juice is another way of ordering food.

explanations.title: Notes
explanations.body: The enclitic naman introduces a related topic: Anong oras naman kayo sarado? means “And how about closing time, what time do you close?”. Dialog A has two sentences that use both long nang and short ng: Bukas po kami nang ika-sampu ng umaga and Sarado po kami nang eksaktong alas-nuwebe y medya ng gabi. The two are pronounced the same (like nang) and come into focus in sentences with adverbial phrases. The short ng in eksaktong alas-nuwebe y medya ng gabi (literally “at exactly 9:30 of evening”) is used as the preposition “in”. For now: use ng when followed by a noun and nang when followed by an adverb or adverbial phrase. Nang and ng will be explained more fully in a future lesson.

explanations.title: Simple adjectives and ma adjectives
explanations.body: Tagalog adjectives may be classified into two kinds according to their structure: simple adjectives (root words) and ma adjectives (ma + root word). To ask the taste of the food, one asks Ano ang (Ano’ng) lasa ng pagkain? Simple adjectives from Presentation 1: Sariwa ang gulay (The vegetable is fresh) and Panis na ang kanin (The rice is already spoiled).

explanations.title: Adjective as a noun modifier

lessons.title: 64. C3 L3 · Clock time in Tagalog and Spanish-derived numbers
lessons.subtitle: ika-sampu ng umaga · alas-nuwebe y medya · menos kinse para alas-nuwebe · sampung minuto bago mag-ala-una

explanations.title: Tagalog and Spanish clock time
explanations.body: Tagalog and Spanish derivative numbers are used for clock times. Spanish derivative numbers are more commonly used in casual conversation or informal writing, while Tagalog is used in more formal settings. To ask the time, one simply asks Anong oras na? Except for ala-una (1:00), the rest of the hours use alas. Patterns: ika- + Tagalog number + ng + time of day, and ala(s)- + Spanish number + ng + time of day. Ika and ala(s) are hyphenated before the number.

examples.text: Bukas po kami nang ika-sampu ng umaga.
examples.translation: We open at ten in the morning.
And what time do you close?

examples.text: Sarado po kami nang eksaktong alas-nuwebe y medya ng gabi.
examples.translation: We close at exactly nine thirty in the evening.

explanations.title: Mag- with clock time
explanations.body: The prefix mag with clock time indicates movement toward a certain time. The mag phrase is preceded by bago, “before”: sampung minuto bago mag-ala-una (ten minutes before one). In other instances bago is not needed, but the first letter of the prefixes ika and ala(s) is repeated: Mag-iika-sampu na ng umaga and Mag-aalas-diyes na ng umaga (it is about to be ten in the morning).

explanations.title: Expressing definiteness
explanations.body: Alas-diyes impunto ng gabi (exactly ten at night) and eksaktong alas-nuwebe y medya ng gabi (exactly nine thirty at night) are definite times. Minutes before or after the hour: menos kinse para alas-nuwebe (15 minutes before 9:00); pasado alas-tres ng hapon (past 3:00 p.m.); mga bandang alas-sais ng gabi (about 6:00 p.m.).

explanations.title: Table: fractions of time (for reference)
explanations.body: The book’s table; spoken alternatives are separated by semicolons. The book misprints alas-ais y medya (it is alas-sais y medya). Menos kuwarto means “a quarter before”, the less common alternative to menos kinse.

lessons.title: 65. C3 L3 · Restaurant listening, speaking, glossary and self-evaluation
lessons.subtitle: Passage 1 and 2 · Ano ang lasa ng pagkain? · Pa-order nga po ng… · Self-evaluation

explanations.title: Passage 1: at a turo-turo eatery (the book’s script)
explanations.body: Key: four items: grilled fish, rice, soup and water. The most expensive is the grilled fish. The free item is the water. The soup costs ₱5.00 per order. (The book’s key says the fish costs ₱70.00, but the script says sesenta pesos, so ₱60.00.)

examples.translation: Woman: How much is the grilled fish?
Man: Sixty pesos, ma’am. (the book’s key says ₱70.00)
Woman: And how much is the rice?
Woman: How much is the soup?
Woman: And how much is the water?

explanations.title: Passage 2: opening days and hours (the book’s script)
explanations.body: Key: the restaurant is open Tuesday to Saturday, from 6:00 a.m. until exactly 8:00 p.m.

examples.translation: Man: What days are you open?
Man: What time are you open?

examples.text: Bukas po kami nang ika-anim ng umaga.
examples.translation: Woman: We open at six in the morning.
Man: And what time do you close?

examples.text: Sarado na po kami nang alas-otso impunto ng gabi.
examples.translation: Woman: We are closed at exactly eight o’clock at night.

explanations.title: Expressions describing food (Activity 9, the book’s script and key)
explanations.body: Key adjectives in order: delicious, fresh, spoiled, gross (fishy smell), sweet, cold, tasty, sour, sweet, salty, bitter.

examples.translation: The fish has a fishy smell.

explanations.title: Two people in a restaurant (Activity 10, the book’s script)
explanations.body: Key: the man’s three questions: what time did you order the food, until what time is the restaurant open, and what time is it now. She ordered past 8:00, the restaurant closes at 9:30 and the conversation took place at exactly 9:00.

examples.text: Anong oras ka nag-order ng pagkain?
examples.translation: Man: What time did you order the food?
Woman: It was already past eight.

examples.text: Hanggang anong oras ang restaurant bukas?
examples.translation: Man: Until what time is the restaurant open?
Man: What time is it now?
Woman: It is now exactly nine o’clock.

explanations.title: Speaking: ordering and asking the taste (Activities 11 to 13)
explanations.body: In a turo-turo eatery, ask your partner about the prices of the dishes and order using the model of Presentation 1; change the underlined parts, and order with Bigyan ninyo nga po ako ng… or Pa-order nga po ng…. Then use the model Ano ang lasa ng pagkain? / Masarap ang pagkain. with the adjectives below. Guided Q and A: A asks the opening time, B says it in Spanish-derived numbers; A asks the closing time, B uses a fraction of time in Tagalog; A asks what time it is, B says it with either system. Second dialog: A asks what time B ordered food (about seven), A asks what time it is now (ten minutes before eight), A asks when the restaurant closes (about ten).

explanations.title: Self-evaluation for Chapter 3
explanations.body: Check that you can: enumerate common Filipino dishes; ask and answer simple questions about meals of the day, ingredients, weights and measures, prices (in Tagalog and Spanish-derived numbers), business hours and clock times; enumerate adjectives for describing food; extract information from reading and listening passages; and transcribe and translate food-related and shopping dialogs. You should have a clear understanding of the linker na, fractions, weights and measures, the question word magkano, Set I demonstrative pronouns, food-related adjectives, and clock times in Tagalog and Spanish-derived numbers. If you are unsure, review that section, find a study partner and ask your team leader for more help.

explanations.title: Activities left out
explanations.body: The audio, the pair work and the written self-evaluation check boxes.
